ap_macroeconomics-m01.stem: Which of the following correctly compares a corporate bond with a share of stock?

options.text: A bond gives ownership of the firm, while a share of stock is a loan to the firm.
options.why: Reverses the two assets; a bond is a loan and a share is ownership.

options.text: A bond is a loan that pays interest and is repaid at maturity, while a share of stock is an ownership claim on the firm.
options.why: Bondholders are creditors; stockholders are owners.

options.text: A bond always has a higher risk than a share of stock.
options.why: Stocks are typically riskier than bonds because stockholders are paid after creditors.

options.text: A bond pays a return that depends on the firm's profit, while a share of stock pays a fixed interest rate.
options.why: Reverses the typical return patterns of the two assets.

options.text: A bond and a share of stock are both forms of money.
options.why: Stocks and bonds are financial assets, not money.

ap_macroeconomics-m01.stem: Which of the following assets is the most liquid?

options.text: A ten-year government bond.
options.why: A bond must be sold, and its price can change, so it is less liquid than cash.

options.text: Cash held in a wallet.
options.why: Cash can be used immediately without any loss of value, so it is the most liquid asset.

options.text: A certificate of deposit with a penalty for early withdrawal.
options.why: The penalty makes the certificate less liquid than cash.

options.text: A share of stock in a large firm.
options.why: A stock must be sold first, which takes time and can involve a loss, so it is less liquid than cash.

options.text: A rental house.
options.why: Selling real estate takes time and costs, so it is much less liquid.

ap_macroeconomics-m01.stem: Which of the following correctly describes the relationship between risk and return on financial assets?

options.text: Risk and return are unrelated for financial assets.
options.why: Ignores that investors require higher returns for greater risk.

options.text: Government bonds are always riskier than corporate bonds.
options.why: Government bonds are generally lower risk than corporate bonds.

options.text: Assets with higher risk generally must offer a higher expected return to attract buyers.
options.why: Investors require compensation for bearing risk.

options.text: Assets with higher risk generally offer a lower expected return.
options.why: Reverses the risk-return trade-off.

options.text: Assets with higher liquidity must offer a higher return than assets with lower liquidity.
options.why: Reverses the liquidity relationship; illiquid assets usually must offer higher returns.

ap_macroeconomics-m02.stem: Which of the following is true of the long-run Phillips curve (LRPC)?

options.text: It is downward sloping, so policymakers can permanently lower unemployment by accepting higher inflation.
options.why: Describes the short-run trade-off as if it were permanent.

options.text: It is vertical at the natural rate of unemployment, so there is no long-run trade-off between inflation and unemployment.
options.why: In the long run unemployment returns to the natural rate whatever the inflation rate is.

options.text: It shifts whenever aggregate demand increases.
options.why: An AD change moves the economy along the SRPC; the LRPC shifts only when the natural rate changes.

options.text: It is horizontal at the natural rate of inflation.
options.why: The LRPC is vertical, not horizontal.

options.text: It is upward sloping because inflation raises unemployment in the long run.
options.why: Describes stagflation in the short run, not the long-run curve.

facts: variant=Which of the following is true

options.text: Unemployment stays permanently below the natural rate.
options.why: Ignores that expectations adjust and the SRPC shifts.

options.why: Does not follow from expansionary policy once expectations adjust.

options.text: Unit of account.
options.why: Describes the use of money as a common measure of value, not the situation given.

options.text: Medium of exchange.
options.why: Accepted in exchange for goods and services.

options.text: Barter.
options.why: Barter is exchange without money, the opposite of the situation described.

options.text: Store of value.
options.why: Describes holding money to keep purchasing power over time, not the situation given.

options.text: Standard of deferred payment only.
options.why: Describes the use of money to settle debts, which is not the situation given.

ap_macroeconomics-m04.stem: The economy is in a recessionary gap, and the government takes no action. Which statement best describes how the economy returns to long-run equilibrium?

options.text: Nominal wages rise because of high unemployment, shifting short-run aggregate supply to the left.
options.why: High unemployment puts downward pressure on wages.

options.text: Input prices fall because of high unemployment, shifting short-run aggregate supply right until output returns to potential.
options.why: Slack in resource markets lowers input prices, which shifts SRAS right and raises real GDP back to full employment.

options.text: The price level rises and real GDP stays below potential permanently.
options.why: Self-correction lowers the price level while real GDP rises toward potential.

options.text: Aggregate demand shifts right automatically, because lower real GDP raises consumption.
options.why: The self-correction works through the supply side, not by a shift in AD.

options.text: Long-run aggregate supply shifts right, because the gap increases potential output.
options.why: A gap does not change potential output.

ap_macroeconomics-m05.stem: A country's currency appreciates. Which of the following best explains the likely effect on the country's real GDP in the short run, other things equal?

options.text: Exports become cheaper to foreigners and imports become more expensive, so net exports rise and aggregate demand shifts to the right.
options.why: Reverses the effect of an appreciation on relative prices.

options.text: Exports become more expensive to foreigners and imports become cheaper, so net exports fall and aggregate demand shifts to the left.
options.why: Net exports are a component of aggregate demand.

options.text: Aggregate supply shifts to the left, so real GDP falls.
options.why: The main short-run effect works through aggregate demand.

options.text: Exports and imports both rise, so aggregate demand is unchanged.
options.why: An appreciation changes relative prices in opposite directions for exports and imports.

options.text: Net exports do not change, because exchange rates affect only financial assets.
options.why: Exchange rates affect the prices of traded goods.

options.why: Reverses the effect of a depreciation on net exports.

options.why: A rightward AD shift raises the price level along SRAS.
